title: Peace over precision (Yevamot 65b)
hookLine: the Talmud notes God softened Sarah's words to Abraham to keep peace (Genesis 18:12–13)
last: DON'T MAKE A FACE GO WHITE.

lines: WHAT DID SHE SAY ABOUT ME?
cards: Say your sister says something sharp about your husband. Not cruel, just unguarded. Later your husband asks: what did she say about me?
You could repeat it word for word. That would be precise. Or you could pass on only the part that wasn't sharp, and leave the rest unsaid.
Which one is right? The Talmud noticed that God faced this exact situation, in the book of Genesis, and made a choice you might not expect.

teach.h: SARAH LAUGHS: MY LORD IS OLD.
teach.b: In Genesis, three visitors tell Abraham that his wife Sarah, in her old age, will have a son.
Sarah is listening from inside the tent, and she laughs to herself: now that I'm worn out, will I have pleasure, "my lord being old also?"
Then God speaks to Abraham: why did Sarah laugh and say, will I really have a child, now that I'm old? Notice what changed. Sarah said, my husband is old.
God reports, I'm old. The part about Abraham is gone.
In tractate Yevamot, the school of Rabbi Yishmael points this out: great is peace, for even the Holy One changed Sarah's words for its sake.
The same page teaches that a person may change a detail for the sake of peace, and one sage even says it's a mitzvah.
It isn't a license to lie whenever it's convenient; the same tradition prizes truth, and later teachers debate exactly how far this goes.
It's about a narrow kind of moment: when repeating someone's words exactly would only wound, and wouldn't help anyone.
There, the Talmud says, choose peace. Leave out the sharp part. You don't have to invent anything.
Often, just like in Genesis, it's enough to not repeat the thing that hurts.

how: Jewish ethics prizes shalom bayit, peace in the home, and teaches both honesty and restraint in speech; the rules against gossip, lashon hara, discourage repeating hurtful words at all.

games.q: your husband asks what your sister said about him. she said something sharp. what do you do?
o: share what's true and kind, and leave out the sting.
games.why: the Talmud learns from Genesis: God left out Sarah's words about Abraham, for the sake of peace. nothing was invented.

practice: Think of something someone said to you recently about someone else: a complaint, a sharp comment, a bit of gossip. Ask: if I pass this on word for word, does it help anyone, or only hurt?
Picture keeping the true and useful parts, and leaving the sharp edge behind.

wordCard.voice: Sarah, whose words about Abraham's age God quietly edited when retelling them, leading the Talmud to say: great is peace.

carryVoice: Your line: keep the peace. Even God left a line out, for the sake of peace. See you tomorrow.
